overview: Two of the three classic routes bacteria use to pick up new DNA from their surroundings — one grabs free DNA, the other gets it delivered by a virus.

aspects.label: Overview / Core Definition
aspects.valueA: Uptake of naked, free DNA fragments from the environment by a competent bacterial cell.
aspects.valueB: Transfer of bacterial DNA from one cell to another via a bacteriophage acting as the vector.

aspects.label: Source of Transferred DNA
aspects.valueA: Free DNA released into the environment, often from lysed bacterial cells.
aspects.valueB: Bacterial DNA accidentally packaged into a phage capsid during phage assembly.

aspects.label: Key Requirement
aspects.valueA: Recipient cell must be naturally competent, or be made competent artificially in the lab.
aspects.valueB: Requires a bacteriophage capable of infecting the donor and recipient bacteria.

aspects.label: Type Classification
aspects.valueA: Not applicable in the same way — transformation is a single mechanism.
aspects.valueB: Classified as generalized (any random DNA fragment packaged) or specialized (specific genes near a prophage integration site).

aspects.label: Laboratory Relevance
aspects.valueA: Basis for standard molecular cloning techniques (e.g. heat-shock or electroporation of plasmid DNA into E. coli).
aspects.valueB: Historically important for mapping bacterial chromosomes; relevant to how virulence genes (e.g. some toxins) spread between strains.

aspects.label: Examples
aspects.valueA: Streptococcus pneumoniae's natural transformation, discovered in Griffith's classic experiment.
aspects.valueB: Phage-mediated transfer of the diphtheria toxin gene in Corynebacterium diphtheriae.

aspects.label: Key Distinguishing Feature
aspects.valueA: Direct uptake of free environmental DNA.
aspects.valueB: DNA delivered via a bacteriophage vector.
